ta-l1d3q3-d1e97.summary: A divisio textus for the part of Distinction 3 in which Lombard shows the Trinity and unity through the image in the human mind. Thomas divides it into the substance of the image, what the image consists in, and the ascent from the image to the Trinity. He follows Lombard's assignment of the image first in the powers (memory, understanding, will) and then in the habits (mind, knowledge, love). He reconstructs the arguments for the powers' equality from their mutual inclusion: memory holds itself and whatever is known and willed, understanding contains everything not unknown, and the will, as universal mover, uses all. He notes Lombard's handling of the objection that properties and mutually related powers cannot be one essence, and the dissimilarities between image and exemplar, such as the human being with the three powers being one person. He also traces the similarities in the second triad: distinction in unity, procession (mind as parent, knowledge as offspring), and equality. Two articles are announced: on the subject of the image and on its parts.
claims: The image is assigned first in the powers of memory, understanding, and will, then in the habits of mind, knowledge, and love.
The equality of the three powers is shown by their mutual inclusion.
The image is dissimilar to the Trinity, e.g. in being one person.

ta-l1d3q3-d1e180.summary: First objection that the mind is not the only subject of the image. Augustine finds an image of the Trinity in bodily sight, in the external thing, its image in the eye, and the seer's intention joining them, and bodily sight does not belong to the mind.
claims: Augustine finds a trinity in bodily vision.

ta-l1d3q3-d1e183.summary: Second objection. Damascene places the image in free choice, which does not seem to belong to the mind.
claims: Damascene locates the image in liberum arbitrium.

ta-l1d3q3-d1e186.summary: Third objection. Augustine says the image is to be sought in that part of the soul than which it has nothing better, which seems to be higher reason, clinging to the eternal things to be contemplated. So the image is in higher reason.
claims: The image is in the best part of the soul, apparently higher reason.

ta-l1d3q3-d1e193.summary: Fourth objection. Dionysius says the angel is a divine image, so the image is not only in our mind.
claims: Dionysius calls the angel an image of God.

ta-l1d3q3-d1e199.summary: Contrary objection that the image is in no creature. Hilary defines an image as a distinct and unique likeness of one thing equaling another, and no creature equals the Creator.
claims: An image is a likeness that equals what it images, and no creature equals God.

ta-l1d3q3-d1e202.summary: Thomas's determination. An image differs from a vestige: a vestige is a confused and imperfect likeness, while an image represents a thing more determinately, in all its parts and their arrangement, so that something of its interior can be perceived. So only those creatures that by their nobility imitate and represent God more perfectly are called his image, namely angels and humans, and in humans according to what is noblest in them. Other creatures approach the character of image more or less as they participate more or less in God's goodness.
claims: An image represents more determinately than a vestige, revealing something of the interior.
Only angels and humans, in their noblest part, are images of God.

ta-l1d3q3-d1e205.summary: Reply to the first objection. Augustine shows likenesses of the Trinity in many things, but a perfect likeness only in the powers of the mind, where there is consubstantial distinction and equality. The three factors of sight are not consubstantial, so he places the image only in the mind.
claims: Only in the mind's powers is there a consubstantial distinction with equality, as required for the image.

ta-l1d3q3-d1e208.summary: Reply to the second objection. Free choice cannot hold a perfect likeness, since it has no distinction of powers, and it is not the soul's highest part, being only operative, whereas the contemplative is nobler. Damascene uses 'image' broadly for any likeness. Free choice imitates God insofar as it is the first principle of its works and cannot be coerced.
claims: Free choice is not the seat of the image properly speaking, since it lacks a distinction of powers and is operative rather than contemplative.
Free choice resembles God as an uncoercible first principle of its works.

ta-l1d3q3-d1e211.summary: Reply to the third objection. Higher reason clings to eternal things as the rule and norm of action, directing our works by divine reasons. The image is not there but in the part that contemplates eternal things in themselves.
claims: The image lies in the part that contemplates eternal things in themselves, not in higher reason as practical.

ta-l1d3q3-d1e215.summary: Reply to the fourth objection. The image of the Trinity can be considered in three ways. (1) As express representation of the divine attributes: since divine goodnesses shine more abundantly in angels, the angel is a more express image ('signaculum', Ezek. 28, per Gregory). (2) As representing the distinction of persons: the likeness is more express in humans, whose powers are more distinct. (3) As God is the principle of things: the image is found in humans and not angels, since one human is the principle of all humans and the soul is wholly in the whole body as God is in the world. Since the latter representations concern externals, it must be granted simply that the angel is more in God's image than the human.
claims: Angels are more expressly the image of God with respect to the attributes and simply speaking.
Humans image the distinction of persons more expressly, and God as principle in a way angels do not.
concepts: soul in the body as God in the world

ta-l1d3q3-d1e218.summary: Reply to the contrary objection. The image is found differently in the Son and in creatures, as a king's image is in his son and on a coin (Augustine). The Son is the perfect image, representing the Father perfectly; a creature falls short of the perfect character of image as it falls short in representation. So the creature is called 'image' and 'to the image', which is not said of the Son. A creature need not equal the Creator simply, which is true only of the Son, but equals him in a qualified sense as it represents him in a qualified sense.
claims: The Son is the perfect image; creatures are imperfect images 'to the image'.
Creatures equal God only in a qualified sense, proportionate to their qualified representation.

ta-l1d3q3-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Question 3 maps Lombard's treatment of the image of the Trinity in the mind: its substance, its assignment in the powers and then in the habits, the proofs of equality from mutual inclusion, the objections about properties and relations, and the dissimilarities. It announces articles on the subject and the parts of the image.

ta-l1d3q3-Dd1e172.summary: Article 1 asks whether the mind alone is the subject of the image. Objections propose bodily sight, free choice, higher reason, and the angel, and a contrary objection denies that any creature is an image, since none equals God. Thomas distinguishes the image from the vestige as a more determinate representation and restricts the image to angels and humans in their noblest part. Augustine's other trinities lack consubstantiality, and free choice lacks distinction of powers and is operative rather than contemplative. The image lies in the contemplation of eternal things in themselves. Angels image the attributes more expressly and are simply more in God's image, while humans better image the distinction of persons and God as principle. The Son alone is the perfect, equal image, and creatures are imperfect images 'to the image'.
claims: The image of God is in angels and in the human mind, the noblest part of the soul.
The angel is simply more an image of God than the human, though the human better represents the distinction of persons.
Only the Son is the perfect image; creatures are 'to the image'.

ta-l1d3q3.summary: Quaestio 3 of Book I, Distinction 3 begins the treatment of the image of the Trinity in the human mind, after the vestige. The Prooemium analyses Lombard's two Augustinian triads (memory–understanding–will and mind–knowledge–love) and his proofs of the equality of the powers from their mutual inclusion. The single article locates the image in rational creatures, angels and humans, in their noblest, contemplative part. The image differs from the vestige by its determinate representation of interior features, and a trinity qualifies as an image only where there is consubstantial distinction and equality. Comparing angels and humans, the angel is simply more in God's image, while the human better represents the distinction of persons and God as principle. The Son alone is the perfect image equal to the Father.
claims: The image of the Trinity is found only in rational creatures, in their contemplative mind.
An image requires determinate representation with consubstantial distinction and equality.
The Son alone is the perfect image; creatures are images 'to the image'.
